question: I have been sued as a director. Will the company pay my defence costs, and when?
aliases: does the company have to indemnify a director California
Corporations Code 317 advancement of expenses undertaking
who pays defense costs for a director lawsuit
mandatory indemnification successful on the merits California
can a corporation indemnify a director in a derivative suit
shortAnswer: Four different things get called the company paying, and they arrive at different times. Section 317(d) is mandatory but only where the agent has been successful on the merits, and then only for expenses actually and reasonably incurred [S:ca-corp-code-317]. Section 317(b) and (c) are permissive, on a good faith standard, and have to be authorised by one of four routes in subdivision (e) [S:ca-corp-code-317]. Section 317(f) allows expenses to be advanced before final disposition, but only against an undertaking to repay if entitlement is ultimately not established [S:ca-corp-code-317]. And section 317(i) lets the corporation insure the agent whether or not it would have the power to indemnify that liability at all [S:ca-corp-code-317].
assumes: You are a director, officer, employee or other agent of a California corporation, which is how section 317(a) defines agent [S:ca-corp-code-317]. If the entity is an association managing a common interest development, a different framework applies and is noted below [S:ca-civ-code-5800].
You are asking what the statute permits and requires, not what your own articles, bylaws or indemnity agreement say. Those documents sit on top of the statute and this record has not read yours.
You are asking about the mechanism rather than the merits. Nothing here says whether you met any standard of conduct or whether any particular expense is recoverable.
why:
The reason this question is hard to answer in one sentence is that the statute contains four separate mechanisms and people use one phrase for all of them. Take them in the order they matter to somebody who has just been served.

What happens now. Section 317(f) permits expenses incurred in defending a proceeding to be advanced before final disposition, upon receipt of an undertaking by or on behalf of the agent to repay that amount if it shall be determined ultimately that the agent is not entitled to be indemnified [S:ca-corp-code-317]. This is the only limb that produces money while the case is running, and notice what it is: an advance against a promise to repay. Not a payment. If entitlement is not established at the end, the money comes back, and it comes back at the worst possible moment, which is immediately after losing.

What happens if you win. Section 317(d) is the one mandatory provision in the section: where an agent has been successful on the merits, the agent shall be indemnified against expenses actually and reasonably incurred [S:ca-corp-code-317]. Shall, not may. But read the trigger. It is success on the merits, and it operates at the end. As a source of funding during a two-year defence it is worth nothing; as an entitlement it is the strongest thing in the section, and it is the only limb that does not run through the authorisation machinery.

What happens if you neither win nor lose outright. Then you are in the permissive limbs. For a proceeding other than a derivative action, section 317(b) permits indemnification where the agent acted in good faith and in a manner the person reasonably believed to be in the best interests of the corporation, and in a criminal proceeding had no reasonable cause to believe the conduct was unlawful [S:ca-corp-code-317]. For a derivative action, section 317(c) permits indemnification against expenses where the agent acted in good faith and in a manner the person believed to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders [S:ca-corp-code-317].

And permissive means somebody has to decide. Section 317(e) sets out who: a majority vote of directors who are not parties to the proceeding, a written opinion of independent legal counsel, approval of the shareholders with the shares of the person to be indemnified not counted, or the court in which the proceeding is pending [S:ca-corp-code-317]. Look at the first of those against a realistic claim. In a matter where most of the board has been named, a majority of non-party directors may not exist, and the route quietly closes. This is the part worth working out before it is needed rather than during.

There are also places the corporation simply cannot go. Section 317(c) restricts indemnification in a derivative action in respect of claims where the person has been adjudged liable to the corporation, and where a settlement has not been approved by the court [S:ca-corp-code-317]. So the two outcomes that most need funding, being held liable to the company and settling with it, are the two the indemnity is least able to reach.

Which is exactly where the fourth mechanism comes in, and it is the reason directors and officers insurance is not a duplicate of the indemnity. Section 317(i) permits a corporation to purchase and maintain insurance on behalf of an agent against liability asserted against or incurred by the agent in that capacity, whether or not the corporation would have the power to indemnify the agent against that liability under this section [S:ca-corp-code-317]. Whether or not it would have the power. The statute contemplates insurance covering things the corporation is forbidden to indemnify. A director who has read the indemnification article in the bylaws and stopped there has read the narrower of the two instruments.

One definitional point that pays for itself. Section 317(a) defines expenses as including without limitation attorneys' fees and any expenses of establishing a right to indemnification [S:ca-corp-code-317]. The cost of arguing about whether you are entitled is itself within the definition of expenses. It also defines proceeding as any threatened, pending or completed action or proceeding, whether civil, criminal, administrative or investigative [S:ca-corp-code-317], so a regulatory or investigative matter that never becomes a lawsuit is inside the section.

Underneath all four mechanisms sits the standard the good faith conditions are judged beside. A director must perform the duties of a director in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders, and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances [S:ca-corp-code-309]. Care including reasonable inquiry, in terms. A director may rely on officers or employees, on counsel, independent accountants or other persons as to matters believed to be within their professional or expert competence, and on a committee of the board upon which the director does not serve, but only without knowledge that would cause such reliance to be unwarranted [S:ca-corp-code-309]. A person who performs the duties in accordance with both of those subdivisions shall have no liability based upon any alleged failure to discharge the person's obligations as a director [S:ca-corp-code-309]. Which is to say the record of what the board asked, and of whom, is doing work in this question long before any indemnity is claimed.

One last thing if the board in question is a homeowners association rather than a business corporation, because the framework inverts. For a qualifying volunteer officer or director of an association managing a residential or mixed use common interest development, section 5800(a) provides protection from personal liability in excess of the coverage of insurance, subject to conditions [S:ca-civ-code-5800]. One of those conditions is that the association maintained and had in effect the specified policies both at the time the act or omission occurred and at the time a claim is made [S:ca-civ-code-5800]. There the insurance is not a backstop to the protection. It is a precondition of it, and it is a precondition the individual director does not control.
whatChanges: Whether the proceeding has ended, and whether it ended in success on the merits, since that is what makes section 317(d) mandatory [S:ca-corp-code-317].
Whether the claim is derivative, because section 317(c) restricts indemnification where the person is adjudged liable to the corporation or a settlement is not court-approved [S:ca-corp-code-317].
Whether a majority of directors who are not parties still exists, since that is the first of the four authorisation routes [S:ca-corp-code-317].
Whether an undertaking to repay has been given, which is the condition on advancing expenses before final disposition [S:ca-corp-code-317].
Whether the corporation carries insurance, since section 317(i) permits cover for liability the corporation could not itself indemnify [S:ca-corp-code-317].
What the articles, bylaws or any indemnity agreement provide, which this record has not read and which sit on top of the statute.
Whether the entity is a business corporation or an association under Davis-Stirling, because the second runs on a conditional protection instead [S:ca-civ-code-5800].
variability: Both Corporations Code sections are quoted from the official host [S:ca-corp-code-317][S:ca-corp-code-309], as is the Civil Code section [S:ca-civ-code-5800]. Nothing here is corroborated by a second source, and the sections should be read directly before anything is relied on.

This record describes the statutory baseline only. A corporation's articles, bylaws or a separate indemnity agreement may provide differently, and section 317 does not describe what any particular company has agreed to do.

Nothing here establishes whether any agent met the standard of conduct in section 317(b) or (c), whether any expense was actually and reasonably incurred, or whether a proceeding ended in success on the merits. Those are determinations made in the proceeding [S:ca-corp-code-317].

Nothing here states what any directors and officers policy covers. Those forms are not publicly filed and this record has read none. Section 317(i) establishes that a corporation may buy such insurance, not what any insurer agreed to pay [S:ca-corp-code-317].

Indemnification of directors is a matter of the law of the state of incorporation. This corpus holds no indemnification statute for any other state, so nothing here describes the position of a corporation formed outside California.
nextActions: Ask the company for the indemnification article of the bylaws and any indemnity agreement in your name, since the statute is the floor and those documents are what the company has actually promised.
Ask whether expenses will be advanced under section 317(f) and on what undertaking, because that is the only limb that produces funds while the matter is live [S:ca-corp-code-317].
Work out now which of the four authorisation routes is still available, given how many directors are parties [S:ca-corp-code-317].

Ask whether the corporation carries directors and officers insurance and get the policy read by someone independent, since section 317(i) allows it to reach where the indemnity cannot [S:ca-corp-code-317].
Assemble the record of what the board asked and relied on, because reasonable inquiry and the limits on reliance are part of the standard itself [S:ca-corp-code-309].
If the board is an association under Davis-Stirling, confirm the required policies were in force both when the act occurred and when the claim was made [S:ca-civ-code-5800].
author: Aaron Bollinger

handoff.reason: Whether a standard of conduct was met, which authorisation route remains open, and what the company has separately agreed in its bylaws or an indemnity agreement are all determined on documents and facts this record has not seen. A director being sued needs their own counsel, separate from the company's, because the company's interest and the director's diverge precisely where indemnification is restricted.
